metadata.section: Section B: Macroeconomics, Money & Financial Conditions

series_manifest.label: Real Fed Interest Rate (Rate Minus Inflation)

events.label: Fed cuts its rate to near zero
COVID: GDP 7.4% below a year earlier

explanation.summary: The "real" interest rate is the Fed's rate minus inflation. When it is far above zero, borrowing is expensive and the economy slows. When it is below zero, money is effectively cheap. This chart compares it with economic growth.
explanation.methodology: Real federal funds rate = effective federal funds rate (FRED FEDFUNDS) minus year-over-year CPI-U inflation (BLS). Real GDP growth is the change from the same quarter a year earlier (BEA via FRED, A191RO1Q156NBEA), filled to monthly with straight lines.

key_findings.title: 1981: The Hardest Brake
key_findings.description: The real interest rate reached +9.5%, the highest on the chart. A deep recession followed, from July 1981 to November 1982.
key_findings.significance: Very high real rates stopped inflation but also stopped growth.

key_findings.title: March 2022: The Deepest Negative Rate
key_findings.description: The Fed's rate was near zero while inflation was about 8.5%, so the real rate fell to -8.3%, the lowest on the chart.
key_findings.significance: Money had never been this cheap in real terms.

key_findings.title: 2023-2024: Brakes On, Growth Continues
key_findings.description: The real rate rose to about +2.4%. Growth still held near 3% a year. As of mid-2026 the real rate is about -0.6% and growth about 2.2%.
key_findings.significance: Unlike 1981, high real rates did not cause a recession this time.
